I thought this was terrific.

You managed to keep my interest throughout, despite the frankly un-glamorous and unexciting subject matter, and you provided satisfactory reasons (to me, at least) why the Foundation would use Type-blues, which just opens up all this new, intriguing world of possibilities. Above all, though, your writing - the regular pacing, the way each paragraph flows smoothly into the next - made reading this a pleasure.

Easy upvote.

item.content:encoded:
The narrator is very clearly a human with a very human kind of speaking and manner. The narrator has reasonable interactions with the people that they're orienting.

However, the issue of orientations is that it is very difficult to convey any real pacing, climax, or tension. Things that make me care. Such often comes off as the transcript to a lecture. In context, it literally is something of a lecture. It's an orientation. And that's a real struggle for me, because I still can't get invested because by its nature its lacking in things that would make me care.

Downvoted, with apologies.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
No, I'm pretty sure that this being less interesting than Moose's thing is a matter of mathematical fact. Moose's thing has wizards. Mine has people complaining about stuff.

But as for the label of exposition dump… well, that's fair, too. However, I did attempt to do something with this that wasn't the bog standard "Here's what we do (as narrated by a guy who rolls up his sleeves and sits backwards on a chair because he's so cool and sardonic)." The information that's presented here isn't exactly breaking news; a significant amount of it is covered in the other Orientation. Rather, it's the way that it's conveyed that (I think, hopefully) makes it interesting.

The narrator is frazzled and unsure, sniping sarcastically at members of the team (who snipe back just as sarcastically, presumably). There are promises that are made which are explicitly broken in later tales. There is a great deal of dissent among the members of Sigma-3 about whether their team should even exist in the first place. The narrator tries desperately and, to an extent, succeeds in framing the entire thing as compatible with the Foundation's narrative. There is stuff going on here beyond just "this is a thing that happened k." A new identity is slowly being created for the unseen (unread?) members of the team.

Moose and I actually tried to work together to create two different pieces that worked in tandem. "Sweet Christ, we will never use magic" to "hey, we use magic now!" is a rather significant shift, and one which hopefully provokes a few questions. I was intending to write a tale or two about how this happened, but real life got in the way of that. Hopefully I will fill in this rather large gap soon. Not that you should include "Things Gaffs never got around to doing" in your scoring rubric.

But yeah, that's what I intended. Whether or not I succeeded depends on the opinion of each individual reader, but if I didn't, it was a failure of execution, not of intention.

e: Since this is basically an author post, I would like to take the time to mention that this is best read after Lessons Learned, and before Nothing Says Promotion Like a Bag Over Your Head.

SCP-2975, Magic Orientation, and The Conspiracy Of Sigma 3 should not be read by anyone who values their time or has taste.

It's interesting how, when you're part of a highly conservative organization in which everything abnormal is locked up and humanity is punished for its own good on its daily basis, the thought of going against your objective elicits gasps from the room.

I thought this was good, especially because it made that conflict seem complex and interesting, rather than boiling it down into shallow shades of "we gotta do what we gotta do".

+1
